Frecknall's ravishing and mercilessly introspective production... no one is safe from the turmoil rattling their psyches.
Theatrically sizzling if emotionally tepid Broadway revival of “Cabaret.”
Too often I thought the same of the show itself.
At this “Cabaret,” nobody ever forgets their troubles, onstage or off.
Sadly, I also had a better time there than I did during the performance itself.
The revival of 'Cabaret' at the Kit Kat Club transforms the Theatre into an immersive experience.
Redmayne is the reason to see this production, though as captivating as his performance is, he cannot rescue this misguided revival on his own.
Here you have one of the sexiest shows ever written as weirdly afeared of eroticism as it is of actual vulnerability.
Life’s too short for this Cabaret.

It’s an unforgettable, immersive experience that lures audiences in with visions of sweet, sweet hedonism before bowling them over with a harrowing, unflinching tale that will have them reflecting on present day parallels and their place within the world long after they leave the theater.
The team has produced a stunning feat the likes of which Broadway has not experienced in a while.
Rankin's is an extraordinary performance that raises the production to new heights.
Rebecca Frecknall’s production reinvents this 1966 show so that you may feel that you have never seen it before.
However, it all makes for an exciting, edgy, and painstakingly-detailed production.
If you do drink away at this Cabaret, prepare for a mean hangover.
It’s easy to get caught up in the spell of this Cabaret, which is all about mood from the moment you enter down a dumpster-lined alley (we promise, it gets prettier).
It feels most powerful when simply getting down to the basics.
True, not everything about this “Cabaret” is perfectly marvelous, but there’s more than enough to warrant a visit!

In any case, this Cabaret doesn’t always trust the material, but there are also times when it breathes life into the show, becoming powerful as its “go for broke” approach increasingly hits the jackpot.

Despite the stellar Gayle Rankin’s best efforts to inject the latest revival with a sense of urgency as star performer Sally Bowles, director Rebecca Frecknall’s production, now on Broadway after winning multiple awards in London, stays stagnant.
If so much of it weren’t so out of balance, this fourth Broadway revival of “Cabaret” would be impressive in its complete transformation of Kander and Ebb’s great musical.
In this production even the idea of beauty is squashed before it has a chance to slither out into the light.
Because Redmayne isn’t playing a character but rather a symbol of decadence, he presents nothing but a jumble of mannerisms.

Because Frecknall shocks us the entire evening, we emerge from the Kit Kat Club, dazed and numbed rather than horrified at what happened in Germany in the '30s and what could easily be repeated here in the US, or anywhere.
direction that spells out the subtext and telegraphs the show's outcome early and often.
The result is a superficial fairytale of a Berlin overrun with hooker clowns and cartoon Nazis, something that bears little resemblance to the insidious creep of authoritarianism in our own world.
Redmayne, Rankin, and a smartly conceived Cabaret reboot shoot warning flares high into the sky.
It was a magical evening at the theatre. I was absolutely delighted and dazzled by hearing some of these words as if for the first time even though I knew them well.
This reimagining of the classic musical leans heavily into sexual decadence at the expense of its political undertones.
The triumph of this iteration is how it anticipates its audience, teasing them with frothy liberation before making them gasp at Nazi armbands and shattered windows.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this immersive revival: some praise Redmayne and Rankin's performances and the stunning theater transformation, while others feel the elaborate pre-show spectacle and directorial choices overshadow the musical's darker themes.

vs.sum: The August Wilson Theatre offers good sightlines from most seats, although the rake isn't steep, which can cause issues if seated behind taller patrons. The theater has average comfort with decent legroom but tight seats. Its Italian-inspired design and cozy feel enhance the ambiance, making it a pleasant venue overall. Facilities are adequate, with standard amenities and helpful staff.

acc.note: Stair lift to orchestra; elevator between orchestra and mezzanine. Infrared headsets available.
